# Eiffel Tower Opens in France: Explore Its Historic Inauguration and Iconic Design

The Eiffel Tower opened in Paris, France, on May 6, 1889, during the Exposition Universelle. Designed by Gustave Eiffel, it is 330 meters tall and weighs 10,100 tons. The tower symbolizes France and celebrates the centennial of the French Revolution, attracting millions of visitors each year.

During its inauguration, over 2 million visitors attended the event. This impressive turnout highlighted the tower’s appeal and its significance as a symbol of modernity. The Eiffel Tower soon became a centerpiece of the 1889 Exposition Universelle, celebrating the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution. Today, it represents not only the city of Paris but also French artistic and architectural ambition.

Exploring the Eiffel Tower’s popularity reveals how it transformed from a controversial structure to a beloved landmark. Its design influenced future towers around the world. The next section will delve into the tower’s role in popular culture and how it has inspired artists, filmmakers, and architects through the years.

Table of Contents

## What Was the Significance of the Eiffel Tower’s Opening in 1889?

The significance of the Eiffel Tower’s opening in 1889 lies in its architectural innovation, cultural impact, and international representation.

The Eiffel Tower’s opening marked a pivotal moment in both architecture and society, allowing for various perspectives on its significance.Architectural Innovation:  
The Eiffel Tower demonstrates architectural innovation through its use of wrought iron. This material allowed for the tower’s lightweight yet sturdy structure. Gustave Eiffel’s design was revolutionary. The tower, standing at 300 meters, surpassed all existing buildings. Its engineering techniques set a precedent for future skyscrapers.

Cultural Symbol:  
The Eiffel Tower became a cultural symbol of France. It represents Paris’s artistic spirit and innovation. It also reflects the industrial age’s progress, embodying the changes occurring in society. The tower hosts millions of visitors annually, connecting them to French culture and history. It serves as an emblem of national pride and identity.

Economic Boost:  
The Eiffel Tower provided an economic boost to Paris. It attracted tourists and stimulated local businesses. The 1889 Exposition Universelle, where the tower was unveiled, saw over 2 million visitors. This influx generated considerable revenue for the city. The tower remains a vital component of Paris’s economy, contributing billions to tourism.

Technological Milestone:  
The Eiffel Tower stands as a technological milestone in engineering. Its construction utilized advanced techniques that were groundbreaking at the time. The use of prefabricated elements allowed for efficient assembly. The tower’s design paved the way for future innovations in iron and steel architecture.Source of Controversy:  
The tower’s construction stirred controversy. Initially met with skepticism, many artists and intellectuals criticized its design. Prominent figures like Guy de Maupassant and Alexandre Dumas expressed their disdain. Over time, however, public opinion shifted positively, culminating in the tower’s acceptance as an iconic structure.

In summary, the Eiffel Tower’s opening in 1889 serves as a transformative moment in architecture, culture, economy, technology, and societal conversations, shaping how we view iconic landmarks today.

## How Did Gustave Eiffel Envision the Tower’s Design and Purpose?

Gustave Eiffel envisioned the Eiffel Tower as a symbolic structure representing modern engineering and showcasing France’s industrial prowess. He sought to create a landmark that balanced aesthetics with structural integrity.

Eiffel’s key design concepts included:

Modern Engineering: Eiffel aimed to demonstrate the capabilities of iron construction. The tower utilized over 18,000 iron parts. This construction showcased the strength and flexibility of iron, aligning with the technological advances of the late 19th century.

Aesthetic Appeal: Eiffel prioritized artistic design alongside functionality. The tower’s lattice structure gave it an intricate appearance while minimizing wind resistance. This design provided both beauty and stability, essential for a towering structure. [...] Public Enthusiasm: Many Parisians celebrated the tower as a symbol of modern engineering. Crowds gathered to witness the opening ceremony on March 31, 1889.

Cultural Optimism: The tower represented France’s technological progress and artistic ambition. It was seen as a centerpiece for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, showcasing France’s prowess to the world.

Critical Voices: Notable intellectuals, including writers like Guy de Maupassant, criticized the structure. They viewed it as an eyesore that disrupted the Parisian skyline.

Global Attention: International reactions varied from admiration to disbelief. Many foreign visitors expressed awe during the exposition, highlighting the tower’s unique design and height, which was unprecedented at the time.

Economic Impact: The Eiffel Tower attracted millions of visitors. According to the Société d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel, it has welcomed over 300 million visitors since its opening, proving its draw as a tourist attraction.

Architectural Significance: Designed by Gustave Eiffel, the tower marked a turning point in engineering. It utilized iron in novel ways, influencing future architectural designs globally.

In summary, the Eiffel Tower’s inauguration sparked both excitement and criticism, unifying different perspectives on innovation and aesthetics in Paris and around the world.

## What Lasting Impact Did the Eiffel Tower Have on French Culture and Identity?

The Eiffel Tower has a lasting impact on French culture and identity by serving as a national symbol, a hub for tourism, and a canvas for artistic expression.

Main Points:  
1. National Symbol  
2. Tourism Magnet  
3. Artistic Inspiration  
4. Cultural Controversy

These points illustrate the multifaceted impact of the Eiffel Tower on French culture and identity.

National Symbol:  
The Eiffel Tower embodies French pride and innovation. It was constructed for the 1889 Exposition Universelle (World’s Fair) to celebrate the centennial of the French Revolution. According to the French Ministry of Culture, the tower represents architectural progress and the spirit of French resilience. Over time, it has become a symbol of France itself. Tourists and locals alike often associate the tower with national identity and Parisian culture.

Tourism Magnet:  
The Eiffel Tower attracts millions of visitors each year. In 2019, it welcomed around 7 million tourists, making it one of the most visited paid monuments in the world. This influx of visitors significantly contributes to the Parisian economy. The tower’s presence boosts local businesses, from restaurants to souvenir shops. A study by Paris Tourism found that the tower generates substantial revenue and supports numerous jobs in the hospitality sector, emphasizing its economic significance.Artistic Inspiration:  
The Eiffel Tower has inspired countless artists across various mediums. It appears in literature, film, and visual art, symbolizing romance and the beauty of Paris. Renowned artists like Claude Monet and filmmakers like Woody Allen have featured the tower in their works, showcasing its cultural significance. The tower has become a muse for creative expression, embodying the essence of cities and art in modern culture.

Cultural Controversy:  
The Eiffel Tower’s construction faced significant backlash, with critics decrying its design as an eyesore. Assessing differing perspectives, architect Charles Garnier referred to it as “a tower that would shape modernity.” However, the initial controversy has given way to a broader appreciation. This contentious history highlights the evolving nature of cultural acceptance and identity in France, showing that national symbols can emerge from, and sometimes transform, public opinion.

Overall, the Eiffel Tower’s impact on French culture and identity encompasses pride, economic benefits, artistic influence, and evolving perceptions, making it a vital part of France’s historical and contemporary landscape.

## How Has the Eiffel Tower Evolved Since Its Inaugural Opening?

The Eiffel Tower has evolved significantly since its inaugural opening in 1889. Initially, it served as a temporary structure for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, celebrating the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution. In 1909, the French government considered dismantling it; however, it remained due to its value as a radiotelegraph station. Over the years, the tower underwent various modifications. In the 1930s, the addition of lighting provided a new visual appeal. The 1980s brought modern elevators and enhanced visitor facilities. In recent years, sustainable practices emerged, such as solar panels and energy-efficient lighting. Currently, the Eiffel Tower stands as a global symbol of Paris and attracts millions of visitors annually. Its continued innovation demonstrates how it adapts to modern needs while preserving its historic significance.

## What Fascinating Facts Should You Know About the Eiffel Tower’s History?

The Eiffel Tower’s history is rich with fascinating facts that reflect its significance as a cultural and architectural landmark.

Transitioning from these pivotal points leads us to a deeper exploration of the Eiffel Tower’s history.

Construction Timeline:  
The Eiffel Tower’s construction timeline indicates that it was completed in 1889. The construction took just over two years, beginning in January 1887 and finishing in March 1889. This ambitious project aimed to showcase French engineering prowess during the World’s Fair, marking the centennial of the French Revolution.Original Purpose:  
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, also known as the World’s Fair. This event celebrated the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution. The structure was intended to highlight France’s industrial advancements and symbolize national pride. While initially seen as a temporary structure, its purpose evolved as it gained recognition.

Height Records:  
The Eiffel Tower was the tallest man-made structure in the world upon its completion. Standing at 300 meters (984 feet), it surpassed the Washington Monument by 41 meters. It remained the tallest structure until the completion of the Chrysler Building in New York City in 1930. This height record contributed to its iconic status.

Design and Architecture:  
The Eiffel Tower’s design showcases innovative iron lattice construction. Engineer Gustave Eiffel, along with Maurice Koechlin and Édouard Nouguier, planned the tower’s design. Its unique framework allowed for significant height with minimal material. Eiffel’s design emphasized both functionality and beauty, setting a precedent for future skyscrapers.

Initial Reactions:  
Upon opening, the Eiffel Tower faced substantial criticism from artists and intellectuals, including prominent figures like Guy de Maupassant. They considered it an eyesore and a blight on Paris’s skyline. These objections highlighted a cultural divide between traditional Parisian aesthetics and the modern industrial approach symbolized by the tower.Modern Use:  
Today, the Eiffel Tower functions as a thriving tourist attraction, welcoming over 7 million visitors annually. It features three observation decks that offer stunning views of Paris. The tower also hosts various events, exhibitions, and light shows, which enhance its appeal in contemporary culture.

Renovations:  
The Eiffel Tower has undergone numerous renovations throughout its history to preserve its structure. Maintenance efforts include painting the tower every seven years to protect it from rust. Recent upgrades have improved visitor facilities and incorporated energy-efficient technologies, ensuring its relevance in the modern era.

These intriguing aspects of the Eiffel Tower’s history illustrate not only its architectural significance but also its evolving role in culture and society.

# The Eiffel tower's inauguration and first visitors

Eiffel Tower

On Sunday 31 March 1889, Gustave Eiffel showed some of the famous personalities of the day who had come to attend the official inauguration ceremony around what was then the tallest tower in the world.

After climbing the 1,710 steps that led to the top of the Tower, they unfurled the French flag to the sound of a 21-gun salute. Gustave Eiffel wrote on a woman's fan: "The French flag is the only one with a 300-metre pole."

The official inauguration of the Eiffel Tower was on May 15th, 1889, the opening day of the Exposition Universelle.

The Eiffel Tower remained the world's highest construction until the Chrysler Building was erected in New York in 1930.

La tour Eiffel et le dôme central - Exposition universelle de 1889 by © Parisienne de photographie - Léon et Lévy / Roger-ViolletEiffel Tower

On May 15th, 1889, the Eiffel Tower welcomes its first visitors.

People from all over the world gathered in the city of Paris to have a look at this masterpiece.

Bassin de la tour Eiffel - Exposition universelle de 1889 by © Parisienne de photographie - Neurdein/ Roger-ViolletEiffel Tower

The 1889 Exposition Universelle in Paris received millions of visitors. Amongst them, 1,953,122 came to see the Eiffel Tower: almost 12,000 a day!

The Tower was an immediate success.

From the very first week, although the lifts were not yet in service (they would be from the 26th May), almost 30,000 visitors climbed the monument using the staircase: a total of 1,710 steps to the top!And still today, the view from the top is as spectacular as it was back then!

Un des magasins de souvenirs de la tour Eiffel - Exposition Universelle de 1900 by © Parisienne de photographie - Neurdein / Roger-ViolletEiffel Tower

All sorts of boutiques (sale of souvenirs, photographers’  booths, binocular rental, refreshments) and restaurants opened up on the monument.

The main Parisian places are indicated and allow visitors to locate themselves from the top of the Tower.

Now, monuments from all over the world are indicated.

On the first floor, four restaurants, each in a different style, were installed: the Russian restaurant, the Anglo-American bar, the French restaurant and the Flemish restaurant.

From the outset, the lifts allowed hundreds of thousands of visitors to climb the Tower safely to embrace the whole of Paris.

Never before had the limits of such heights and loads been broken.

Two of the original lifts are still in service on the Eiffel Tower today. Carefully preserved, this exceptional heritage still testifies to Gustave Eiffel’s visionary genius.

A universal Tower of Babel, almost 250 million visitors of different ages and origins have come from all over the planet to see the Tower since it was opened in 1889. As France’s symbol in the world and the showcase of Paris, today it attracts almost seven million visitors a year, making it the world's most popular paid-entry monument.

Conception—Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel

Since its inauguration, the Iron Lady has triggered fierce emotions– between disenchantment and passion, disillusion and adoration. It has gradually become ingrained in French culture and history. Whether wrapped in the blanket of the morning dew or bathed in the glowing red light of the sunset, the monument is today endlessly appealing, attracting nearly seven million visitors a year. Festive celebrations all year long Adventure Game On March 30th, the Eiffel Tower launched a free Adventure Game for visitors. Dive into an immersive treasure hunt to unlock the mystery of the iconic monument’s history. A portrait exhibition An exhibition of giant portraits tells the story of all the skilled men and women who operate the Eiffel Tower each day. It’s a unique opportunity to learn about the daily lives of each man and woman working every day, day after day, with a diversity of skilled trades and jobs. Their goal? To make the monument even more beautiful, even more iconic. The exhibition is displayed outdoors on the palisades surrounding the North elevator until the end of the year. Themed treats and tickets To mark the special anniversary year, the Eiffel Tower’s pastry chefs have designed two tasty tarts– one flavored with lemon, the other with chocolate. They are topped with a white chocolate dot displaying the anniversary logo. Your Eiffel Tower admission ticket will also celebrate the 130th anniversary– decorated with the special birthday colors. The summer terrace Since April, the summer terrace has been enticing visitors- and it has a new decoration, a nod to the 130th anniversary of the Eiffel Tower. The Eiffel Tower Design Prize For its 130th anniversary, the Eiffel Tower Operating Company (SETE – Société d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel) launched a design competition (Prix Design tour Eiffel) in collaboration with the Ateliers de Paris. The competition offered an exceptional opportunity for designers and creatives to showcase their savoir-faire to make the Eiffel Tower shine even more brightly. The project could be an everyday consumer item or an exceptional creative object or patterns that can be reproduced in a limited edition. The three winning projects will be unveiled as part of Paris Design Week, on September 14, 2019, on the occasion of a special evening at the Gustave Eiffel Salon, located on the 1st floor of the monument. An astounding Light Show for the Eiffel Tower’s second major event in history On May 15th, 1889, the Eiffel Tower opened to the public for the very first time…only a few days after its inauguration at the World’s Fair. On May 15th, 2019, the Iron Lady opened its gates to 1,300 children and organized a concert on the Esplanade. When night fell, the Iron Lady dressed up with an unparalleled light and laser show to retrace its history, from its birth up to the present day. The show also gave a magnificent and a [...] “I ought to be jealous of the Tower. She is more famous than I am.” – Gustave Eiffel

When it was built in 1887, not everyone had a crush on the iron structure. The project was not only criticized by local residents but also– and especially!– by the art community. Forty-seven artists including the renowned writers Guy de Maupassant and Emile Zola as well as the Opera’s famous architect, Charles Garnier, signed a petition published on February 14, 1887, protesting the construction of the “useless and monstrous” Eiffel Tower. All of them claimed that it would “dishonor” the beauty of Paris. Paul Verlaine even compared the tower to a “belfry skeleton!” The project showcased real technical prowess as the ground along the river was water-drenched. It attracted two million visitors at the World’s Fair in 1889.

Since its inauguration, the Iron Lady has triggered fierce emotions– between disenchantment and passion, disillusion and adoration. It has gradually become ingrained in French culture and history. Whether wrapped in the blanket of the morning dew or bathed in the glowing red light of the sunset, the monument is today endlessly appealing, attracting nearly seven million visitors a year.
